intro: A box puzzle is a stack of seven or eight boxes and about six clues. Most teaching for it stops at "find a fixed box, connect the clues, eliminate". That is true, but it is too general to make you fast. These lessons are built from the puzzles themselves.

**What I studied first.** Ten real clerk-level puzzles from memory-based papers (IBPS Clerk 2020, 2023, 2024, 2025; SBI Clerk 2022 and two from 2025; RRB Clerk 2021 and two from 2025), and 32 single-stack sets from your bank. Each was written out as exact conditions and solved by a script, so every number below was counted and none is a guess.
| What was measured | Real papers (10) | Your bank (32) |
| Number of boxes | 8 in IBPS and recent SBI Clerk, 7 in RRB Clerk | 8 in 17 sets, 7 in 7, 9 or 10 in 7, 6 in 1 |
| Puzzles that fix a box's place outright | 1 | 3 |
| Puzzles with no clue about a single box at all | 6 | 12 |
| Ways the main block fits, typically | 2 or 3 | 2 or 3 |
| Open cases when clues are taken in printed order | about 8 | about 8 |
| Open cases when the block is built first | about 4 | about 3 |

**What this means.** There is usually no fixed box to begin with, so the puzzle has to be started from the clues that lock boxes to each other. That is what the ten lessons teach, one piece at a time. Every worked example is a real paper puzzle, and every practice set comes from your bank with a full walk-through.

A note on honesty: memory-based papers are reconstructions by candidates. All ten puzzles used here have exactly one arrangement when checked by script, which is good evidence that they were remembered correctly, but the exact wording may differ slightly from the exam.
after: That is the single-stack box puzzle, which is the only kind found in the clerk-level papers studied. The **Quick revision** tab keeps the short tables.
For every set, the order is the same: short notes, hub, block, shapes, count the fits, columns, mirror and room clues, closers, then check one unused clue before answering.

Still to come for this topic, as insurance: boxes with a second fact (a colour or an item in each box), a vacant shelf, and two stacks side by side. None of the clerk papers studied had these, though your bank and the PO papers do.

lessons.title: Turn every clue into a number
lessons.plain: The starting point. Number the stack from the bottom, and read each clue as "so many places apart". Nothing is placed yet.
teach: A box puzzle gives you seven or eight boxes "kept one above another" and a handful of clues. Before any solving, there is a small language to learn. Each clue, however it is worded, says one of only a few things, and each of those is a **number**.

**Number the places from the bottom.** Place 1 is the lowest box. In a stack of 8, place 8 is the top. (If the puzzle itself says "the top box is numbered 1", follow the puzzle. One real paper did that.)
Now the clue words. Call the number of places between two boxes their **step**.
| The clue says | What it means | Step |
| X is immediately (or just) above Y | no box between them | X is 1 above Y |
| Only two boxes are between X and Y | two boxes sit in the middle | 3 apart, either way round |
| X is three boxes above Y | count three places up from Y | X is 3 above Y |
| X is adjacent to Y | next to each other | 1 apart, either way round |
| X is above Y | somewhere higher | not known |
Two of these are confused all the time, so please look at them once more:
- **"Two boxes between"** is a step of **3**. Add one to the number in the clue.
- **"Two boxes above"** is a step of **2**. Use the number as it is.

You may wonder whether "three boxes above" could mean three boxes in between. I checked rather than guessed. In your bank, 14 single-stack sets use this wording. Read as a plain step, every one of them has exactly one arrangement, and in each set I checked against its answer key it is the keyed one; read the other way, most of them have no arrangement at all. In the three real papers where the final arrangement is known (IBPS Clerk 2024, SBI Clerk 20 and 21 September 2025), the same reading fits. So you can rely on it.
**Clues that count boxes above or below.** These give a place directly.
| The clue says | Place, in a stack of N |
| Only two boxes are below X | place 3 |
| Only two boxes are above X | place N - 2 |
| As many boxes above X as below X | the middle place (only when N is odd) |

The habit this lesson is building: as you read each clue, write it in short form beside the puzzle, such as **T = R + 2** or **W, R: 4 apart**. From the next lesson on, you will solve from these short notes and hardly look at the sentences again.

example.q: Write each clue of this real puzzle as a number. (IBPS Clerk Prelims, 4 October 2025, shift 1, as candidates remembered it.) Three boxes are placed between W and R. T is placed two boxes above R. P is placed just below T but above W. Two boxes are placed between P and V. S is placed three boxes below V. Q is placed adjacent to W.
steps: Three boxes between W and R: **W, R are 4 apart** (which is higher is not said).
T two boxes above R: **T = R + 2**.
P just below T: **P = T - 1**. And P is above W: no number, keep it aside.
Two boxes between P and V: **P, V are 3 apart**.
S three boxes below V: **S = V - 3**.
Q adjacent to W: **Q, W are 1 apart**.
example.answer: Six short notes. You will solve this same puzzle from them in the next lesson.

check.q: In a stack of 8 boxes numbered from the bottom, "only two boxes are kept above X". Where is X?
check.why: Two boxes above X means places 7 and 8 are above it, so X is at place 6. (Place 3 would be "two boxes below X".)

more.q: Only three boxes are kept between P and Q. P is at place 2. Where is Q?
more.why: Three boxes between means a step of 4. 2 + 4 = 6. (Place 5 uses a step of 3, which would leave only two boxes between.)

more.q: R is kept three boxes above S. S is at place 2. Where is R?
more.why: "Three boxes above" is a step of 3, used as it is: 2 + 3 = 5.

more.q: In a stack of 7 boxes, as many boxes are above M as below M. Where is M?
more.why: Three above and three below: the middle, place 4. A real RRB Clerk paper (7 December 2025) opened with exactly this clue.

more.q: In a stack of 7, more than two boxes are kept between X and Y, and X is at place 1. Where can Y be?
more.why: More than two between means three or more between: a step of at least 4. From place 1 that is place 5, 6 or 7.

lessons.title: The block: join the clues before touching the stack
lessons.plain: New: do not look for a box to place. Join the clues that share a box into one rigid block, away from the stack.
teach: Most advice for puzzles begins with "find the fixed clue and place it first". For box puzzles at clerk level, that advice usually has nothing to work on.

I checked 10 real clerk-level puzzles (IBPS Clerk, SBI Clerk and RRB Clerk, 2020 to 2025) and 32 sets in your bank. **Only one paper puzzle in the 10, and three bank sets in the 32, tell you outright where a box is.** Six of the 10 paper puzzles give no clue at all about a single box's place.
So the puzzle has to be started another way. Here it is.

**Clues that share a box can be joined.** If T = R + 2 and P = T - 1, then all three are locked together: P = R + 1. You do not yet know where they are in the stack, but you know exactly how they sit **relative to each other**. That locked group is a **block**.
**How to build it.**
- Pick the box that appears in the most clues. Call its place 0.
- Take each clue that mentions a box already in the block, and write the new box as a number above (+) or below (-) the 0.
- When a clue allows two ways ("4 apart" can be +4 or -4), see whether the block already rules one out: the spot may be taken, or a plain "above" clue may forbid it.
- Keep going until no remaining clue touches the block.

Then look at the **height** of the block: from its highest box to its lowest, counting both. If the height equals the number of boxes in the stack, the block **is** the stack, and the puzzle is finished without a single case.
This is not rare. In the 2025 IBPS Clerk puzzle below, seven of the eight boxes fall into one block that fills the stack.

example.q: Solve the IBPS Clerk Prelims puzzle of 4 October 2025 (eight boxes P, Q, R, S, T, U, V, W) from the notes of the last lesson: W, R are 4 apart. T = R + 2. P = T - 1, and P is above W. P, V are 3 apart. S = V - 3. Q, W are 1 apart.
steps: R is in two clues and T links to P, so start there. Let R = 0. Then T = +2 and P = +1.
W is 4 from R: +4 or -4. But P is above W, and P is at +1. So W cannot be at +4. **W = -4.**
V is 3 from P (+1): +4 or -2. S = V - 3. If V = +4, S = +1, which is P's spot. So **V = -2 and S = -5.**
The block now runs from T (+2) down to S (-5). That is 8 places: the whole stack. So T is at place 8 and S at place 1.
Fill in: T 8, P 7, R 6, V 4, W 2, S 1. Q is next to W: place 3 (place 1 is S). U takes place 5.
example.answer: Top to bottom: T, P, R, U, V, Q, W, S. No cases were needed.

check.q: P is two boxes above Q. R is just below Q. Three boxes are between P and S, and S is below P. How many places does this block take, from its top box to its bottom box?
check.why: Let Q = 0. P = +2, R = -1, S = P - 4 = -2. The block runs from +2 to -2: five places.

shortcut.title: Which box to start from
text: Start the block from the **hub**: the box named in the most clues that give an exact step (immediately, n between, n boxes above).
A quick way to find it: as you write the short notes, put a tick over a box's letter each time it appears. The letter with the most ticks is the hub.
In the 17 bank sets practised in these lessons, the main block holds about 4 of the boxes on average. That is half the puzzle done before the stack is drawn.

lessons.title: Sliding the block up and down
lessons.plain: New: the block is shorter than the stack. Count how many places it can sit in, draw one column for each, and let the other clues remove columns.
teach: Last lesson the block filled the whole stack. More often it is a little shorter, so it can **slide**.
**How many places can it sit in?** A block of height H in a stack of N boxes fits in
**N - H + 1 ways.**
A block 7 tall in a stack of 8 fits 2 ways: touching the top, or touching the bottom. A block 6 tall fits 3 ways.

This is the number of **cases** you face, and you know it before drawing anything. In the 32 bank sets and 10 real paper puzzles I worked through, the main block most often fits in **2 or 3 ways**. Working clue by clue in the order they are printed, the same puzzles typically reach about 8 open cases at their worst point. That difference is the time this method saves.
**What to do.**
- Draw one column for each fit, side by side, with the block written in.
- In each column, list the free places.
- Take the remaining clues one at a time and ask of each column: can this clue still be satisfied with the free places left? Strike out a column the moment the answer is no.

The best clues for striking out columns are the ones that need **room**: "U is immediately above Q" needs two free places next to each other; "two boxes between L and K" needs two free places 3 apart; "I is above F but below K" needs free places in a certain order. Look at the free places, not at the letters.

example.q: SBI Clerk Prelims, 20 September 2025, shift 2 (eight boxes F, G, H, I, J, K, L, M). J is three boxes above M. Two boxes are between L and K. G is just below J. Two boxes are between M and H. I is above F but below K. More than two boxes are between G and L.
steps: Block from J: G = J - 1, M = J - 3. H is 3 from M: that is J itself (taken) or J - 6. So H = J - 6.
Height from J down to H: 7 places. In a stack of 8 it fits 8 - 7 + 1 = 2 ways.
Fit 1, block touching the top: J 8, G 7, M 5, H 2. Fit 2, block touching the bottom: J 7, G 6, M 4, H 1.

Fit 2: free places 8, 5, 3, 2. L and K are 3 apart: (8, 5) or (5, 2). G is at 6 and L must be at least 4 away from it, so L = 2 and K = 5. Free: 8 and 3. I is below K, so I = 3, and F must be below I: nothing free. Fit 2 is out.
Fit 1: free places 6, 4, 3, 1. L and K 3 apart: (6, 3) or (4, 1). L is at least 4 from G (place 7): L = 3 with K = 6, or L = 1 with K = 4.
K = 4, L = 1 leaves 6 and 3; I must be below K, so I = 3, and F below I has no place. Out. So K = 6, L = 3, then I = 4 and F = 1.
example.answer: Top to bottom: J, G, K, M, I, L, H, F.

check.q: A block is 6 places tall. The stack has 8 boxes. In how many ways can the block sit in the stack?
check.why: N - H + 1 = 8 - 6 + 1 = 3: with its top at place 8, 7 or 6.

shortcut.title: Read the free places, not the letters
text: After the block is in, write the free places of each column as plain numbers, for example **free: 6, 4, 3, 1**. Then test the remaining clues against those numbers:
- "immediately above" needs two free numbers that differ by 1;
- "two boxes between" needs two free numbers that differ by 3;
- "X above Y above Z" needs three free numbers, and tells you which box gets the highest.
A column where the needed pair of numbers does not exist is dead at once. You do not have to try any letters in it.

lessons.title: When the block can take more than one shape
lessons.plain: New: a "between" clue does not say which box is higher, so the block may flip. Plain words like above, below and top settle it.
teach: A clue such as "three boxes between S and V" gives a step of 4 but not the **direction**. V may be 4 above S or 4 below. So a block with such a clue in it can have two shapes, and each shape slides on its own.
Before you draw columns for every shape, let the cheap clues work. Three kinds of clue choose the shape for you.
**1. A plain "above" or "below" about two boxes already in the block.** "P is above W", with P at +1: W cannot be at +4. These clues look weak, but inside a block they are exact.
**2. The edges of the stack.** A shape that is taller than the stack cannot exist. Work out the height of each shape; often one of them is 9 tall in a stack of 8.
**3. Clues about the top or bottom.** "At least two boxes are above C" or "D is not at the bottom" cut off the highest or lowest fits of a shape.
So the order of work is: build the block, write down each shape it can take, strike out shapes with rules 1 to 3, and only then slide what is left.
The real papers often give this partner clue in the very next sentence ("Two boxes are between B and G. G is below B."), so look for it straight away.

example.q: RRB Clerk (Office Assistant) Prelims, 8 August 2021 (seven boxes A to G). Two boxes are between B and G. G is below B. A is just below G. More than three boxes are between A and E. C is not above G. Two boxes are between F and C.
steps: B, G are 3 apart, and "G is below B" gives the direction at once: G = B - 3. Then A = G - 1 = B - 4. One shape only.
Height from B to A: 5 places. In a stack of 7 it fits 3 ways: A at place 3, 2 or 1.
"More than three between A and E" is a step of at least 5. With A at 3, E would need place 8. Out.
A at 1: then G is at 2, and C must be below G. Only place 1 is below, and A has it. Out.
A at 2: G 3, B 6, and E = 7. C is below G: place 1. F is 3 from C: place 4. D takes 5.
example.answer: Top to bottom: E, B, D, F, G, A, C.

check.why: Let K = 0, so M = +1. L is at +4 or -4. If L were at +4 it would be above M. So L = -4: four places below K.

lessons.title: The mirror clue: as many above X as below Y
lessons.plain: New: one clue that looks vague and is in fact exact. The two places always add up to one more than the number of boxes.
teach: "As many boxes are kept above N as below G." This clue appears in more than half of the bank sets (18 of 32) and, in one form or another, in three of the ten real papers. It looks loose. It is one of the strongest clues in the puzzle.

Think of a stack of 7. If N is at the top, no box is above it, so no box is below G: G is at the bottom. If N is second from the top, G is second from the bottom. The two boxes sit at **mirror** places.
In numbers: **place of N + place of G = number of boxes + 1.**
| Stack | The mirror pairs |
| 7 boxes (sum 8) | 1 and 7, 2 and 6, 3 and 5 |
| 8 boxes (sum 9) | 1 and 8, 2 and 7, 3 and 6, 4 and 5 |
Three things follow, and each one saves time.
- **The moment one of the two is placed, the other is placed too.** So in every column of your block, the partner's place is forced. If that place is already taken by the block, the column is dead.
- **In a stack of 7 they can never both be at place 4**, since they are different boxes. In a stack of 8 the pair 4 and 5 are neighbours.
- The box named after "above" is the higher one whenever the count is less than half. "As many above N as below G" with only one or two boxes above N means N is near the top and G near the bottom.

**Variations.** "The number of boxes above S is two more than the number below V": work out the count for one and add two. "As many boxes above M as below M" (the same box): M is exactly in the middle.

example.q: RRB Clerk Prelims, 6 December 2025, shift 2 (seven boxes A to G). Three boxes are between B and D. A is immediately below B. The number of boxes below A is the same as the number above G. One box is between G and C, and C is above G. E is not at the bottom.
steps: Mirror clue in a stack of 7: place of A + place of G = 8.
Short notes: B = A + 1. B, D are 4 apart. C = G + 2.
Run A through its places. A 6: G 2, B 7, D 3, C 4. All different. Keep.
A 5: G 3, B 6, C 5, which is A's place. Out. A 4: G would be 4 too. Out.
A 3: B 4, and D would need place 8 or 0. Out. A 2: G 6, C 8. Out. A 1: G 7, C 9. Out.
So B 7, A 6, C 4, D 3, G 2. Free: 5 and 1. E is not at the bottom: E 5, F 1.
example.answer: Top to bottom: B, A, E, C, D, G, F.

check.q: In a stack of 8 boxes, as many boxes are above X as below Y. X is at place 6. Where is Y?
check.why: The places add up to 9. 9 - 6 = 3. (Check: two boxes are above place 6, and two are below place 3.)

shortcut.title: Use the mirror first when it touches the block
text: If one of the two mirror boxes is in your block, do not wait. As soon as the columns are drawn, write the partner's forced place in each one.
In all four practice sets of this lesson it removes at least one column on the spot, before any other clue is read.
To find the partner without thinking: partner's place = (number of boxes + 1) - this place. In 8 boxes: 9 minus. In 7 boxes: 8 minus.

lessons.title: Soft anchors: even, odd, prime, not at the top
lessons.plain: New: clues about one box that do not fix it but narrow it. Use them to cut the list of places for the block, before drawing columns.
teach: Clerk papers rarely say "T is at place 4". What they do say, quite often, is something softer about one box:
- "T is at an even numbered place"
- "A is kept in an odd numbered place"
- "U is third from either of the ends"
- "at least two boxes are above C"
- "B is not at the top", "E is not at the bottom"
None of these places a box. Each of them **cuts down the places the block can sit in**, and that is how to use them: join the soft clue to the block **before** counting the fits.

"S is at an even place but not below the fourth" leaves 4, 6 and 8. If the block also says V is 3 above S, then S = 8 is impossible (V would be at 11) and S = 6 too (V at 9). One place is left, and you never drew a column.
For quick use:
| Words | Places in a stack of 8 |
| prime | 2, 3, 5, 7 (1 is not a prime) |
| third from either end | 3 or 6 |
| at least two above | 6 or lower |

**Two soft clues on boxes of the same block multiply.** If Q is even and T, three places from Q, is also even, that cannot happen: an odd step changes even to odd. Checking **even against odd** like this is a very fast test. A step of 1 or 3 switches between even and odd; a step of 2 or 4 keeps it.
And the weakest ones, "not at the top" and "not at the bottom": keep them for the very end. In the real papers they are nearly always what decides between the last two boxes.

example.q: SBI Clerk Prelims, 19 November 2022, shift 1 (seven boxes P to V). U is third from either of the ends. P is adjacent to U. Three boxes are between P and S. The number of boxes above S is two more than the number below V. Q is above R, which is not below S.
steps: U is at place 3 or place 5.
P is next to U: 2 or 4 (with U at 3), or 4 or 6 (with U at 5). S is 4 from P.
P at 4 would put S at 8 or 0. So P is 2 or 6: either (U 3, P 2, S 6) or (U 5, P 6, S 2).
Count clue. S at 6: one box above it, so V would have minus one box below. Out.
S at 2: five boxes above, so three below V: V at 4.
Free: 7, 3, 1. Q is above R, and R is above S: R 3, Q 7. T takes 1.
example.answer: Top to bottom: Q, P, U, V, R, S, T.

check.q: Eight boxes. S is at an even numbered place, but not below the fourth. V is three boxes above S. Where is S?
check.why: S can be 4, 6 or 8. V = S + 3 must exist in a stack of 8, so S cannot be 6 or 8. S is at place 4.

lessons.title: Start where the choices are fewest
lessons.plain: New: the biggest block is not always the best start. Count the places each group can take, and begin with the smallest count.
teach: So far the plan has been: build the biggest block, then slide it. In some puzzles the biggest block is small (two or three boxes) and slides in six or seven ways. Starting there would give you seven columns.
The better rule is the general one behind everything so far:
**Begin with the group of clues that leaves the fewest possible places.**
Three kinds of clue are much tighter than they look, and are worth checking before you choose where to begin.

**1. A wide gap.** "More than four boxes between M and T" in a stack of 8 means a step of at least 6. Only three pairs of places allow that: 1 and 7, 1 and 8, 2 and 8. A clue that sounded vague has pinned two boxes to the ends of the stack.
| Clue in a stack of 8 | Pairs of places that allow it |
| more than four between | 3 pairs |
| more than three between | 6 pairs |
| more than two between | 10 pairs |
**2. A mirror clue joined to an exact step.** "S is three above Y, and as many boxes are above S as below R": S can only be at 4, 5, 7 or 8, and each choice places three boxes at once.

**3. A chain of plain "above" clues.** "K is above R, and R is above V" is three boxes in a fixed order. If only three free places are left for them, they are placed with no thought at all. The more boxes in the chain, the earlier it helps.

And then the **closers**: "not adjacent" clues. They never help you start, but they are almost always what removes the last wrong column. Read them last, and check them against every column that is still alive.
In the IBPS Clerk puzzle of 2024 below, starting from the three-box block gives nine columns. Starting from the wide gap gives four, and each one closes quickly.

example.q: IBPS Clerk Prelims, 25 August 2024, shift 3 (eight boxes A, B, F, K, M, P, T, V, numbered 1 at the bottom). P is three boxes above V. Only two boxes are between K and A. More than four boxes are between M and T. B is above F but not at an odd numbered place. T is just below A. F and M are not adjacent. B is not at the top.
steps: Wide gap first: M and T are at 1 and 7, 1 and 8, or 2 and 8.
T has A just above it, so T is not at 8. That leaves four columns: (T 1, M 7), (T 1, M 8), (T 2, M 8) and (T 7, M 1).
T 7, A 8, M 1: K is 3 from A, so K 5. P = V + 3 with free places 2, 3, 4, 6: V 3, P 6. Left: 2 and 4. B above F: B 4, F 2, but F is next to M. Out.
T 2, A 3, M 8: K 6. Free 1, 4, 5, 7: (V 1, P 4) leaves 5 and 7; (V 4, P 7) leaves 1 and 5. B must be even and not at 8: no even place in either. Out.
T 1, A 2, K 5, M 7: free 3, 4, 6, 8. V 3, P 6 only. Left: 4 and 8. B above F would put B at 8. Out.
T 1, A 2, K 5, M 8: free 3, 4, 6, 7. V 3, P 6 leaves 4 and 7: B would be 7, odd. Out. V 4, P 7 leaves 3 and 6: B 6, F 3. F is not next to M. It works.

lessons.title: Same-gap clues, and the midpoint
lessons.plain: New: "as many boxes between A and B as between C and D". Keep it for last, unless the two pairs share a box. Then it is a midpoint.
teach: "The number of boxes between K and M is the same as the number between L and P." This clue names four boxes and gives no step at all. On its own it cannot start anything.

**The usual case: use it last.** By the time the block is placed, one of the two pairs is normally already in the stack. Read off its step. The other pair must have the same step, and you look for two free places that far apart. It works exactly like a "between" clue whose number you find out late.
A very common result is a step of 1: if K and M turn out to be neighbours, there are no boxes between them, so L and P must be neighbours as well.
**The special case: the two pairs share a box.** "As many boxes between B and E as between E and C." Now E is named twice, and this is quite different:
- B and C are different boxes, so they cannot both be on the same side of E at the same distance.
- So E is **exactly halfway** between B and C. One is above E, the other the same number of places below.

That is an exact clue, and it belongs **in the block**. If B is 4 above E, then C is 4 below E. In one of your bank's ten-box sets this single observation makes the block fill the whole stack, and a puzzle that looks like the hardest in the paper is done with no cases.
So when you see a same-gap clue, look first at one thing: is a box repeated? If yes, block. If no, last.

lessons.title: Putting it together: two blocks, and nine boxes
lessons.plain: New: nothing new in the ideas. Two separate blocks have to fit around each other, and the stack may be longer. The same steps, with more care.
teach: Sometimes the exact clues do not all connect. You get **two blocks** of three boxes each, and neither is tied to the other. The SBI Clerk paper of 21 September 2025 was like this.
Do not try to slide both at once. The way through is:
- Build both blocks on the side and note the height of each.
- Place the **taller** one, or the one with a soft anchor or an "above" clue attached. It has fewer fits.

- For each fit, write the free places as numbers, and ask whether the second block's pattern exists among them. A block needing places u, u - 1 and u - 3 either finds those three numbers free or it does not.
- Then the closers.
Most columns die at the third step without any further work, because a second rigid block is very hard to fit into scattered free places.
**Nine and ten boxes.** Your bank has several; the clerk papers I found had only 7 or 8, and the longer stacks appeared at PO level. If you meet one, the method does not change, but judge it first:
- If the main block is 7 or more tall, the long stack is actually **easier**, because the block has very little room to slide.
- If the biggest block is only 2 or 3 boxes and there are five or more loose boxes, it will take over five minutes. In the exam, do the other puzzles first and come back.
A sensible target once the method is familiar: about 3 minutes for the stack and 15 to 20 seconds for each question.

lessons.title: The five questions: reading the answers off quickly
lessons.plain: New: the stack is built. A few habits make the five questions take seconds each.
teach: Once the stack is right, the five questions should be the quickest marks in the section. I sorted the 216 questions asked on single-stack sets in your bank, and the same few kinds keep returning. The real papers ask the same kinds.
| Kind of question | Share in the bank |
| Which box is above, below or at a given place | about 1 in 3 |
| How many boxes between, above or below | about 1 in 5 |
| Four of the five are alike: find the odd one | about 1 in 8 |
| Which statement is true or false | about 1 in 10 |
| As many boxes above X as below which box | about 1 in 12 |
| Rearranged alphabetically, or two boxes swapped | about 1 in 12 |
**Write the place numbers beside the final stack.** Every one of these questions is then a small subtraction, not counting with a finger.
- **Boxes between X and Y** = difference of the two places, minus 1.
- **Boxes above X** = number of boxes minus X's place. **Boxes below X** = X's place minus 1.
- **As many above X as below which box?** This is the mirror: the answer is the box at place (number of boxes + 1 - X's place).

- **Odd one out, given as pairs.** Find the step for each pair. Four pairs share it; one does not. If the steps do not separate them, look at direction (first box above or below the second), and then at even and odd places.
- **Odd one out, given as single boxes.** It is nearly always even places against odd places, or prime places against non-prime.
- **Arranged in alphabetical order, how many stay unchanged?** Write the alphabetical column right beside your stack and compare row by row. Check whether it says from the top or from the bottom.
- **Statements.** Check the shortest statement first; in "which is true" questions you can stop at the first true one unless an option says "both".
One last habit: before answering, test your finished stack against the **one clue you used least**, usually a "not adjacent" one. It takes five seconds and protects all five answers.

example.q: The final stack, from top to bottom, is R, T, V, P, S, W, U, Q (eight boxes). Answer: (1) How many boxes are between T and W? (2) As many boxes are above V as below which box? (3) Which pair is the odd one: R-T, V-P, T-P, U-Q?
steps: Write the places: R 8, T 7, V 6, P 5, S 4, W 3, U 2, Q 1.
(1) T is 7 and W is 3. 7 - 3 - 1 = 3 boxes.
(2) Mirror of place 6 in 8 boxes: 9 - 6 = 3. The box at place 3 is W.
(3) Steps: R-T 1, V-P 1, T-P 2, U-Q 1. The odd one is T-P.
